In the winter of 1853 a survey party camped above the treeline and watched the cold press against the canvas like a hand. Supplies had dwindled to flour, salted pork and a crate of instruments that nobody in camp could repair: a theodolite, a barometer, two chronometers and a bundle of paper charts whose ink had begun to bloom in the damp. Each morning the men carried the theodolite to the ridge, set it on its brass legs and waited for the clouds to thin. On clear days they could see the river bend twice before it vanished into the gorge, and the older hands swore that the second bend lay a full mile farther west than the charts allowed, a claim the surveyor dismissed as camp talk. By February the argument over that bend had hardened into factions. The surveyor insisted the charts were correct and the weather was deceiving them; his assistant, who had spent three seasons on the river, insisted the opposite and produced a notebook of bearings taken at dawn when the air was steadiest. Neither would yield, and the camp divided along lines that had little to do with geography and a great deal to do with who had been appointed by whom. The cook, who had no stake in the dispute, kept a separate ledger of how much flour each faction consumed while arguing, and by March that ledger had become the most reliable record anyone possessed. When the thaw came the party descended without having settled the question, and the bend was surveyed again the following summer by a different crew, who confirmed the assistant's bearings and quietly corrected the charts. The surveyor, it was said, never accepted the correction; he spent the last evening copying the old bearings into a fresh notebook and comparing them against the assistant's figures, finding to his visible irritation that the two sets agreed almost everywhere except at the bend. He had begun, in his quieter moments, to suspect that the quarrel had never really been about the charts at all, and that the assistant's notebook, with its neat columns of dawn bearings, had become a kind of argument in itself, one that no amount of instrument work could answer. Two of the younger men later claimed they had seen the bend from the ridge on a morning so clear that the river seemed to run uphill, though neither could agree on which bend they meant. The party left the ridge with the instruments oiled and wrapped, the tents folded, and the question of the bend still open. On the final morning he called the party together and read out the rules he intended to enforce on the return journey:

Nobody walks alone after dark, every bearing is written down twice, and no one argues about the river until the instruments are packed.
